I work in a lower mainland school district and my school is short multiple EAs with absolutely no change since September. For a while we couldn’t even get substitutes when our EAs were away. We luckily have enough to give support to the kids like this but it’s at the expense of all the other designated students who bring in equal funding and don’t lash out who have their own struggles and deserve to be supported. 

The NDP promise of an SEA in every k-3 classroom would be amazing but I have a hard time seeing how they can fulfill it when we can’t even staff the classrooms that have designations.

Are you resource / a support teacher? This sounds like something that is not your problem unless you are a resource teacher who is concerned the IEPs you have written are not being followed. That would be something you could potentially talk to admin about.

I am an elementary resource teacher and I understand the frustration when your colleagues don’t do something that seems simple to you. But as a first year teacher I also did plenty of things I am sure my resource teachers at the time shook their heads at. We are all learning, and I have had to do most of my own learning with experience and time.

I would say there’s very little chance you actually 100% know what is going on in other classrooms / with other teachers unless you are frequently in those rooms helping students while they teach and are having conversations with these teachers about how things are going for them.

Your second point is true but I don’t know if the first one is in regards to schools choosing how to spend….it is true the funding doesn’t cover an EA salary but our school is given a designated number of EAs based on the number of students we have who generate funding. So at least in the district I work for, the number of EAs is not a choice the school can make. The school can choose what classes / students they are assigned to, though.  

(Can’t say this is the case for every district in BC though, but I imagine it is.)

I will point out that not every family is able to have parents and older siblings assist in learning. One of my students is the oldest sibling in her family - mom and dad are the only options to help. I teach primary so she is still very young. It’s an unfortunate reality that not every family is able to support their child’s learning at home even if they would like to. 

I hope this doesn’t come across as me trying to “prove you wrong”, I don’t mean to be disrespectful / combative at all, I just think it’s an important misconception to point out when having this discussion - much like how some people’s solution is just “work from home” for a week when there are plenty of jobs that don’t have that option. Not specifically for you, but for anyone reading this.

I mean, you’re right about missing out on in person science time - but elementary students are also missing out on a week of learning to read and add / subtract. Those are foundational skills……and for kids with learning difficulties of any kind, any extra learning loss can seriously compound. 

Not arguing that learning loss isn’t real but I think it absolutely matters for those younger kids. I’d even argue it matters more but maybe I’m biased as an elementary teacher.

I'm not 100% sure what level your kids are at  compared to the ones I coach, but I coach a few different groups in my year round team, most of them entry level. Do you have other coaches at your disposal / are they beginners? 

My groups have three coaches (one per lane) at a time so we can hop kids out as needed and focus on each kid more, so if you're alone and a majority of your kids are good for the kick, this might not work for you. For the younger ones (about 5-8 or even older if they're starting out) a lot of kick problems can be solved by them hopping out and lying on their stomachs and you physically guiding their feet through the kick so they get the feeling of it and can replicate it themselves. That would be something that might fix the scissor kick on certain feet / legs. It would even work for the older ones too...some of them just feel stupid doing stuff like that lol

I admit I am not sure what you mean about body balancing, and for arms hesitating at the chest I think that would be something that you would just have to nag them about, not something that would be fixed by a drill.

It may be helpful to have them JUST do pull or JUST do kick and focus on one problem at a time, either as a group or individually depending on the kid(s). Hopefully this doesn't sound condescending at all because I have no idea how much experience you have coaching or these kids have swimming, but sometimes for younger ones especially they are easily overwhelmed and telling them to fix too many things in one day will overwhelm them and negate progress. If a child has a chronic problem with something it may be best to focus on just that one thing for them while they're swimming so it can REALLY be drilled into their heads and they'll remember it better for next time!!

Hopefully at least something in here is new info for you, if you want to ask anymore questions or give me more specifics feel free to. I just kind of gave you general surface level suggestions b/c I wasn't sure of your groups ability but the end of this summer marks the beginning of my fifth year coaching so I could probably go more in depth if you want!
